pages.title: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
INTRODUCTION

The Street Is a Scored World

Every professional world in the Scorer Series has stakes. The loan officer's call can cost someone their home. The cold caller's thirty seconds can cost them their quarter. The BDM's lunch can cost them their pipeline. The stakes are real and the scoring is real in all of them.

The street is different. Not because the PLT scores run differently — they run identically, Profit and Love and Tax moving through every exchange by the same mechanics as every other world in this series. The street is different because in this world, the Tax of a miscalibrated conversation is not a lost deal or a drained relationship. It is, at its extreme, a life. The stakes do not get higher than that. And the scoring does not get more precise than what those stakes produce.

This is why the street is the most honest scored world available to study. In professional environments, the true score is often obscured by courtesy, by institutional norms, by the managed performance of alignment that organizations produce. In the street, the performance budget is zero. The person across from you in a street conversation is reading your score in real time with survival-level accuracy, and they are running their own score with the same precision. There is no managed agreement in this world. There is only what is true and what it costs.

The PLT framework was built by observing all kinds of conversations. The street conversations were among the most clarifying, because the street strips the score down to its essential elements. Profit — what this exchange actually produces and for whom. Love — who is genuinely held, who is genuinely protected, who is genuinely seen versus used. Tax — what is owed, what has been taken without acknowledgment, what accumulates in every relationship until it produces an event that everyone sees and no one admits they could have predicted.

◆

This book is an analysis, not an instruction manual. It scores the conversations of a specific world using the same framework applied to every other world in this series. The characters are composites. The conversations are representative. The scores are real — meaning the mechanics described here are the actual mechanics of how trust is built, how loyalty works and how it breaks, and how the Tax of the street accumulates until it becomes the event that ends things.

The street has always been scored. This book names the scores.

pages.title: PART ONE
pages.html:
PART ONE

The Street

The scored world — what it is, how it runs, what the PLT framework sees in it that other frameworks miss

The Street Score

The street runs on three things that map directly onto the PLT framework: reputation, loyalty, and debt.

Reputation is Profit made permanent. In most professional worlds, Profit is transactional — it accumulates in specific exchanges and is available to be spent or lost in subsequent ones. In the street, Profit calcifies into reputation, and reputation is the durable currency. The person whose exchanges have consistently produced value — who has been reliable, precise, and honest about what they can and cannot do — carries a Profit score that precedes them into every room. The person whose exchanges have been inconsistent — who has produced value sometimes and extracted it other times — carries a reputation that is a liability in rooms they have not yet entered.

Loyalty is Love made binding. In the street, Love is not a sentiment — it is a structural commitment. Loyalty means that your interests and mine are aligned in a way that is not conditional on conditions being favorable. The person who is loyal holds that position when holding it is costly. This is the test. Every relationship in the street is eventually tested by the moment when loyalty has a price, and the price is identifiable. The response to that test is the Love score expressed in its clearest form.

Debt is Tax by another name — and in the street, Tax is tracked with an exactness that most professional worlds do not match. Every obligation is known. Every favor is remembered. Every slight is logged. The street does not operate on the vague accounting of managed relationships — it operates on the precise ledger of a world where the cost of an unacknowledged debt is not a strained relationship but a concrete consequence. Tax in this world does not compound quietly. It compounds loudly, and when it resolves, everyone in the world sees the resolution.

◆

The PLT framework in this world reveals something that is easy to miss from the outside: the street economy is a high-Trust economy. Not in the sense of being safe — it is not safe. In the sense that the transactions that constitute it are built on personal trust rather than institutional trust. There is no contract. There is no legal recourse. There is only the word, and the word is binding in proportion to the reputation that backs it. The street is one of the few remaining economies where the PLT scores — Profit, Love, Tax — are the only mechanism of accountability available. The scoring, therefore, is not incidental to the street. It is the street.

The Eight Characters

The street has eight primary characters. Every conversation in this book involves at least two of them. Every relationship between them is a scored account.

THE CONNECT

The source. The person above who has the thing everyone below them needs. The Connect's Profit score is structural — it is built into their position — which means their Love and Tax scores are what determine the quality of the relationships they have. The Connect who runs on Profit alone produces relationships built on dependence, not loyalty. The dependence is stable until it is not, and when it is not, the Connect discovers that structural Profit without Love produces no protection when the structure shifts.

THE PLUG

The middleman. The person who knows both sides and makes the connection. The Plug's entire value is the intelligence they carry — they know who has what, who needs what, and who can be trusted in what capacity. The Plug scores highest when their intelligence is accurate and their loyalties are clear. The Plug who double-carries — who is serving two parties whose interests are not aligned — is running a Tax account with one or both of them that will eventually resolve in a way that ends their position.

THE BLOCK

The territory holder. The person who runs the day-to-day and knows every person on the ground level. The Block's Love score is the most consequential in the street because they are the person that the people below them are loyal to — or are not. The Block who has genuine Love from the people they run with has protection that money cannot buy and authority cannot produce. The Block who runs on fear alone has compliance that evaporates the moment a better option appears.

THE CUSTOMER

The end of the line. Often underscored in analyses of street dynamics because the Customer's power seems minimal. It is not minimal. The Customer's aggregate behavior determines the Profit of every level above them, and the Customer who is treated with genuine regard — whose experience of the exchange is consistently above their expectation — is the Customer who does not go elsewhere, who refers, who keeps the whole system running. The Customer who is treated as an extraction point goes elsewhere the moment elsewhere is available.

THE WORKER

The person on the ground. The one taking the most exposure for the least Profit. The Worker's loyalty is the most expensive thing in the street and the most consistently undervalued. The organization that underpays its Workers in Profit while expecting their Love is running the highest-Tax account in the street. The Tax resolves in one of three ways: the Worker leaves, the Worker takes, or the Worker talks. All three are expensive. None are surprising to anyone who has been reading the score.

THE COMPETITOR

The person running the same play in the same space. The Competitor relationship is the most misunderstood in the street because it is treated as purely adversarial when the most valuable version of it is adversarial and informational simultaneously. The Competitor who can be read accurately — whose moves can be anticipated, whose position can be understood — is more valuable than the Competitor who has been eliminated. Elimination ends the information. Reading the Competitor keeps it flowing.

THE INFORMANT

The most dangerous character in the street and the one whose emergence is always predictable in retrospect. The Informant does not appear from nowhere. They appear from a Tax account that built to a point where cooperation with an outside authority produced better terms than continued loyalty to an inside one. The Informant is always someone whose Tax account was allowed to compound without address. The score, if it had been read, predicted the outcome.

THE FAMILY

The person who does not know. The most Love-weighted character in the street because they are the one whose wellbeing is the actual motivation beneath the entire operation for most of the people running it. The Family is the Love score made human. Every decision in the street eventually traces back to a Family — the person being protected, the future being built toward, the reason the work has a meaning beyond the work. The Family is also the highest Tax source in the street when the two worlds collide.

pages.title: PART TWO
pages.html:
PART TWO

The Conversations

Eight scored exchanges. The street world in full. Every movement. Every score.

The Connect Call

The conversation that establishes whether the relationship is real or transactional

Trust in the street does not travel through institutions. It travels through people. The Connect call is where two people decide, without saying so directly, whether the relationship they are about to build is one of mutual investment or of mutual use.

Marcus has been vouched for by someone the Connect trusts. This is the first call. The Connect — who goes by Dee — has heard the name. Marcus has heard enough to know this call matters more than he can show.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE READ
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE READ

Dee: "They told me about you."

Not a greeting. An assessment. Dee is not introducing himself. He is telling Marcus that information has already been transferred and that the call's purpose is to evaluate whether the information matches the person.

Marcus: "I appreciate that."

Short. No performance of gratitude. Marcus understood the register.

Dee: "What do you need?"

Also not a question. An invitation to demonstrate whether Marcus knows what he actually needs and can name it without overselling or underselling the ask.

Marcus: "Consistency. Not the biggest number. Something I can rely on. I'd rather have less that's always there than more that's sometimes there."

Dee is quiet for a moment. The answer was not what most people say on a first call. Most people lead with volume. Marcus led with reliability as a value, which is what Dee actually needs from anyone he works with.

Dee: "That's a smart answer."

Marcus: "It's an honest one."

THE SCORE

The Read — Two People Assessing Each Other Simultaneously

PROFIT 72 ▲ 12|LOVE 68 ▲ 10|TAX 20 ▼ 6

MOVE INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER — MOVE 03

Marcus ran Move 03 in the first call's most important moment: instead of performing desire for the largest possible number — which is what Dee has heard from every person who wants access to his level — Marcus transferred specific intelligence about his own values. Consistency over volume. Reliability over size. This is the answer that tells Dee something true about Marcus rather than something designed to impress Dee. Profit builds because the exchange produced real information. Love builds because Marcus's answer demonstrated that he is not trying to extract maximum value from the relationship — he is trying to build one that can sustain. Tax drops because the first call did not create any obligation that cannot be met. Marcus asked for what he can actually use.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE TERMS
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE TERMS

Dee: "Consistency I can do. Here's how it works with me. You don't call me unless something's wrong. You deal with who I tell you to deal with. And if something changes on your end — anything — I hear it from you before I hear it from someone else. Can you do that?"

Three terms. All of them are about information management and loyalty. None of them are about money. Dee is not setting financial terms on the first call — he is setting relational ones. The financial terms come after the relational ones are established.

Marcus: "Yes."

One word. Marcus did not negotiate. He did not qualify. He understood that the terms were not negotiable and that the correct response to terms you can live with is not to demonstrate that you considered them — it is to accept them cleanly.

Dee: "Good. One more thing. The person who vouched for you — that's on them if it doesn't go right. You understand that?"

Marcus: "I understand it. I also won't let it come to that."

Not a promise of perfection. A statement of intention combined with the acknowledgment that the vouchsafe has weight — that someone else's reputation is now partially in Marcus's hands and that Marcus takes that seriously.

THE SCORE

The Terms — Relational Before Financial

PROFIT 80 ▲ 8|LOVE 76 ▲ 8|TAX 14 ▼ 6

MOVE HONEST STRIKE — MOVE 02

Dee ran Move 02 in its clearest form: he named the three requirements directly, without softening, and added the most uncomfortable one last — the explicit acknowledgment that the vouchsafe creates obligation. Most people in this position manage the vouchsafe weight implicitly, allowing it to exist without being stated. Dee stated it. This is the Honest Strike in the street: the thing that is true and carries weight, named clearly so it cannot be misunderstood. Marcus's response — "I won't let it come to that" — is the correct answer because it accepts the weight of the statement without deflecting it. The relationship now has clear terms. The Tax account starts near zero because nothing has been implied — everything has been stated.

pages.title: MOVEMENT THREE THE CLOSE
pages.html:
MOVEMENT THREE THE CLOSE

Dee: "Talk to Ray. He'll set it up."

The call is over. No farewell performance. Dee has made his decision and communicated it in the most efficient possible form: the name of who Marcus deals with next.

Marcus: "Appreciate it."

Also efficient. Marcus did not thank Dee effusively. He did not comment on how the call went. He matched the register of the close and ended the conversation cleanly.

After the call, both parties have what they needed. Dee has assessed Marcus and found him usable. Marcus has accessed the level he needed and done so without creating obligations he cannot meet. The relationship has started from a position that is rare in this world: honest terms, matched expectations, and a Tax account that starts clean.

THE SCORE

The Close — Efficient, Matched, Clean

PROFIT 86 ▲ 6|LOVE 80 ▲ 4|TAX 10 ▼ 4

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

The path forward in a street Connect call is never elaborate. It is the name of who you talk to next and the implicit understanding that the relationship will be evaluated by what follows rather than by what was said in the call. Dee's close is the most concise form of Move 09 in the series: a single name and an implied instruction. Marcus's response is the correct one. The conversation's score is high not because either party was warm or expressive but because both parties were precise, honest, and equal in their register. The street scores precision over performance. This call was precise.

◆

The Loyalty Test

The moment that determines what the relationship actually is

Loyalty in the street is not declared. It is tested. The test is never announced. It arrives in the form of a moment where the person being tested has an option that would benefit them at the expense of the person they are supposedly loyal to, and the score is determined entirely by what they do with that option.

Ray has been working with Jerome for two years. Someone from outside has approached Ray with an offer — better terms, same work. The someone is a competitor of Jerome's. Ray is now in the conversation that determines who he actually is.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE OFFER ON THE TABLE
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE OFFER ON THE TABLE

Ray: "Jerome. Need to talk to you."

Ray called Jerome directly. He did not manage the information or sit on it. He called the same day the offer came.

Jerome: "Talk."

Ray: "Somebody came to me. Offered me something. Better number, same work. I'm not going to take it. But I'm telling you because you need to know somebody's moving on your people."

Two things happening simultaneously: Ray is demonstrating loyalty by declining the offer, and he is demonstrating intelligence by understanding that the offer's significance is not the offer — it is what the offer reveals about who is targeting Jerome's operation.

Jerome: "Who."

Ray: "Darius's people. The one who approached me was somebody I didn't know. But the number they offered — that's not a number someone offers unless they know exactly what I'm currently working with."

Jerome is quiet. Ray has given him something more valuable than the declined offer: he has given him the intelligence that someone inside has been talking.

THE SCORE

The Offer on the Table — Loyalty As Intelligence

PROFIT 88 ▲ 18|LOVE 92 ▲ 22|TAX 8 ▼ 14

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER — MOVES 02 & 03

Ray ran both moves in the same action. The Honest Strike: he disclosed the offer immediately and directly, including the fact that the offer was better — which is the uncomfortable part that most people omit when reporting a declined offer to a boss. The Intelligence Transfer: he went beyond the disclosure of the offer to the analysis of what the offer revealed. Someone had shared internal information. That intelligence is worth more than the offer itself. Love builds 22 points — the highest movement in this conversation — because Jerome has just seen Ray demonstrate that his loyalty is not contingent on conditions being favorable. The offer was better. Ray declined it and disclosed it the same day. This is the Love score at its most direct expression in the street world.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE RESPONSE
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE RESPONSE

Jerome: "You know what this means."

Ray: "Yeah."

Jerome: "I need to know — you're good?"

Not "thank you for telling me." Jerome does not perform gratitude in moments of operational significance. The question is practical: is Ray's position secure, is he exposed by having been approached, is there anything that needs to be managed on Ray's end.

Ray: "I'm good. Didn't commit to anything, didn't tell them anything. They got nothing from me."

Jerome: "I know that. I'm asking about you — not the situation. You good?"

The second ask. Jerome is not checking the operational status — he has heard that already. He is checking on Ray the person, which is a different question and one that Ray did not initially understand Jerome was asking.

Ray: "...Yeah. I'm good."

A beat of silence before the answer. Ray recognized that Jerome was asking something more personal than operational, and the recognition landed.

THE SCORE

The Response — The Second Question Behind the First

PROFIT 90 ▲ 2|LOVE 96 ▲ 4|TAX 6 ▼ 2

MOVE PRESSURE REVEAL — MOVE 06

Jerome ran Move 06 — Pressure Reveal — in the form of the second question. The first question was operational. The second question named the real conversation: not what happened, but how Ray is. The distinction matters enormously in the street, where conversations tend to stay operational because operational clarity is survival. A leader who asks about the person rather than the situation, in the middle of a moment with operational stakes, is demonstrating Love in the most specific way available to them in this world. The Love score reaches its highest point in this movement not because of a dramatic exchange but because of a second question that most people in Jerome's position never ask.

◆

The Debt Conversation

When the Tax account has become impossible to ignore

Debt in the street is not abstract. It is a specific number, owed by a specific person, due by a specific time. The conversation about debt that has not been paid is the highest-Tax single conversation available in this world — and the one where the scoring matters most, because it determines whether the resolution is a repayment or an escalation.

Devon owes. He has owed for six weeks. He has been unreachable for two of them. The person he owes — who goes by Stone — is now sitting across from him. Stone did not come alone, but the person who came with him is outside.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE ACCOUNTING
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE ACCOUNTING

Stone: "Six weeks."

Not a question. Not a threat. A statement of the exact duration of the unaddressed obligation. Stone is not performing anger. He is naming the precise fact of the situation.

Devon: "I know."

Stone: "You know. So tell me what happened."

Stone is offering Devon the floor. Not as a courtesy — as an assessment. What Devon says next will determine whether this is a conversation about a solvable problem or something else.

Devon: "I got hit. Somebody took the whole thing from me. I've been working to replace it and I'm close — I'm not running, Stone. I'm not dodging. I just needed more time to get it right before I came to you."

The admission is complete: what happened, why he went quiet, and why he didn't come sooner. Devon did not minimize or deflect. He disclosed the full situation including the part that makes him look worst — that he stayed quiet while trying to fix it rather than coming to Stone with the problem when it happened.

Stone: "Why didn't you come to me when it happened?"

Devon: "Because I thought I could fix it before you had to know. That was wrong."

THE SCORE

The Accounting — The Full Disclosure

PROFIT 58 ▲ 10|LOVE 62 ▲ 12|TAX 44 ▼ 12

MOVE OWNERSHIP MOVE — MOVE 05

Devon ran Move 05 without qualification. He owned the six weeks, the silence, and the bad calculation that produced the silence. "That was wrong" — three words, no explanation attached. The Ownership Move in the street has to be complete to function. The partial ownership — "I was trying to protect you from knowing" or "I was going to tell you when I had it" — reads as management rather than accountability. Devon said the thing that is hardest to say in this world: I was wrong to stay quiet. Profit begins to recover because Stone now has accurate information. Love begins to recover because Devon's disclosure demonstrates that he is not trying to work an angle — he is trying to be honest in a situation where honesty is more costly than a managed story would have been. Tax has not resolved — the debt is still real — but it has stopped compounding in the worst direction.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE PATH
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE PATH

Stone: "What's close mean?"

Stone did not respond to the apology. He moved directly to the operational question: how close is close, and what does that look like specifically.

Devon: "I have half of it now. I can have the other half in ten days. I'll bring you the half now today and the rest in ten days — I'm not asking you to wait the full amount. Just the second half."

Stone: "Half today. Ten days for the rest."

Devon: "Today. Right now if you want."

Stone looks at Devon for a moment. The specific offer — half immediately, ten days for the rest — is the right structure for this situation. It demonstrates that Devon has the first half available and is not negotiating the whole amount, only the timing of the second.

Stone: "Ten days. If it's day eleven I don't want to have another conversation."

Devon: "It won't be day eleven."

THE SCORE

The Path — Specific Terms, Accepted

PROFIT 70 ▲ 12|LOVE 68 ▲ 6|TAX 28 ▼ 16

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

Devon ran Move 09 in the form of the most specific offer available to him: not a general promise to make it right, but a specific structure — half now, half in ten days — that he could commit to without overcommitting. Stone's response was to accept the structure and name the consequence of its failure precisely: not another conversation. The Path Forward in a debt conversation has to be more specific than the debt conversation itself, because the debt conversation happened because a prior path was not specific enough. Both parties leave with terms that are exactly stated. Tax drops because the obligation is now on a defined timeline. The account is not clear — it will be clear in ten days — but the relationship has been given a specific path to resolution rather than the open-ended uncertainty of the six weeks that preceded this conversation.

◆

The Worker Conversation

What is owed to the people taking the most exposure

The street organization that does not acknowledge the cost its workers carry is running the highest-Tax account in the world. Not because the workers are likely to complain — they are not. Because the Tax accumulates in a register that produces the most consequential resolution available: the moment when the person who has been taking the most exposure for the least return does the math and decides the math does not work.

Khalil has been working the block for Jerome for three years. He has never been short. He has never had a problem that Jerome had to manage. Jerome called this meeting.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE UNEXPECTED MEETING
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE UNEXPECTED MEETING

Jerome: "Three years."

Khalil: "Yes sir."

Khalil came to this meeting without knowing what it was about. His posture is careful — compliant, attentive, giving nothing away until he knows the temperature.

Jerome: "I want to ask you something and I want an honest answer. Not what you think I want to hear. What's it actually like out there right now?"

Khalil's expression shifts slightly. He was expecting an operational conversation — numbers, instructions, a correction. He was not expecting to be asked how it is.

Khalil: "It's... it's harder than it was. Competition is up. It takes longer to move the same amount. We're out there longer hours for the same result."

Jerome: "You're still hitting the number."

Khalil: "We're hitting it. But it's costing more to hit it than it used to."

The most honest thing Khalil has said to Jerome in three years. He said it because Jerome asked directly and in a way that made honesty feel like the expected answer rather than a risk.

THE SCORE

The Unexpected Meeting — The Honest Answer Arrives

PROFIT 74 ▲ 12|LOVE 78 ▲ 14|TAX 20 ▼ 8

MOVE DIAGNOSTIC OPENING — MOVE 03

Jerome ran Move 03 in its leadership form: he asked the question he actually needed the answer to, in a way that made the honest answer possible. "Not what you think I want to hear" is the specific framing that changes the answer. Without it, Khalil says "it's good" and the meeting stays on the surface. With it, Khalil says what is actually true: the same output is costing more input, which is a condition that eventually produces a different output. Jerome heard this. Profit builds because the conversation arrived at accurate operational intelligence. Love builds because Khalil has experienced, for possibly the first time in three years, a leader who asked how it is rather than only checking whether the number is being hit.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE ACKNOWLEDGMENT
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE ACKNOWLEDGMENT

Jerome: "I know it's harder. I've been watching the time it's taking. I called you here because I wanted you to hear from me directly that I see it — and that your number stays the same even if the environment changes. You don't get penalized for conditions you didn't create."

Khalil is still. This is not what he expected Jerome to say.

Khalil: "I appreciate that."

Jerome: "I also want to say something else. Three years without a problem is not nothing. In this world, three years clean is the rarest thing there is. I know what that costs. You get the same from me that I ask from you — I see it."

The acknowledgment is specific. Not "you're doing a good job." Jerome named the specific thing: three years without a problem, in a world where that is exceptionally rare, and the explicit recognition that it costs something.

THE SCORE

The Acknowledgment — Three Years Named Specifically

PROFIT 86 ▲ 12|LOVE 94 ▲ 16|TAX 10 ▼ 10

MOVE EVIDENCE MIRROR + OWNERSHIP MOVE — MOVES 04 & 05

Jerome ran Move 04 — Evidence Mirror — in the form of the specific acknowledgment: he named the evidence of Khalil's reliability and held it up for Khalil to see. "Three years clean is the rarest thing there is" is not a performance of gratitude — it is an accurate assessment of a fact that Jerome has observed and is now stating. Then he ran Move 05: "I know what that costs." He owns his awareness of the worker's burden rather than performing ignorance of it. Love reaches its highest point in this conversation because Khalil has just heard his leader name the specific cost of his loyalty — not the output, but what it takes to produce that output — and acknowledge it explicitly. This is the conversation that does not happen often enough in the street. When it happens, it builds the kind of Love that holds when the conditions that could break it arrive.

◆

The Competitor

The conversation that most people get wrong

The competitor relationship in the street is almost always misread as purely adversarial. The correctly scored competitor relationship is something more complex: two people who understand each other's positions precisely and who have more to gain from that mutual understanding than from the alternative.

Marcus and Darius have been operating in adjacent territory for two years. They have not had a problem. They are now in a conversation that neither of them requested and both of them agreed to.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE MUTUAL ASSESSMENT
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE MUTUAL ASSESSMENT

Marcus: "I know why you wanted to talk."

Darius: "Tell me."

Darius is testing whether Marcus has the intelligence he thinks he has. This is the competitor's diagnostic: reveal that you have been paying attention without revealing how you have been paying attention.

Marcus: "The corner on Seventh. It's in your territory technically but my people have been using the block at the end of it for a year. You're expanding and now that corner is going to matter to you."

Darius: "That's right."

Marcus: "So before it becomes something neither of us wants it to be, you wanted to have a conversation where it's still a conversation."

A beat.

Darius: "You're smarter than people say you are."

Marcus: "People say I'm smart."

Darius: "I meant smarter than that."

THE SCORE

The Mutual Assessment — Intelligence as Currency

PROFIT 80 ▲ 12|LOVE 72 ▲ 8|TAX 16 ▼ 8

MOVE FRAME RESET — MOVE 01

Marcus ran Move 01 before the conversation formally began: he reframed the meeting from a territorial dispute into a conversation between two intelligent people who both understand what they are trying to prevent. By naming Darius's motivation accurately and charitably — "before it becomes something neither of us wants it to be" — Marcus converted a potential confrontation into a joint problem-solving session. Profit builds because both parties have now demonstrated, in the first exchange, that they are operating at the same level of situational awareness. Love builds because the mutual respect implicit in Marcus's accurate read of Darius's motivation is itself a form of regard — it says: I understand your position well enough to know what you are protecting, and I respect that you are trying to solve this before it escalates.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE NEGOTIATION
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE NEGOTIATION

Darius: "Here's what I need. The corner is mine. What you have on the block can stay — I'm not coming for your people. But I need to know the corner is acknowledged as mine."

Marcus: "I can acknowledge that. In exchange I need the block to stay clean. Your expansion doesn't bring heat to my people's side."

Darius: "Your people stay on the block, my people stay on the corner, nobody's business touches the other."

Marcus: "That works."

Neither party celebrated. Neither party performed relief. They found a structure that served both interests and stated it plainly. The conversation moved exactly as far as it needed to and stopped.

Darius: "One more thing. What happened with your guy — the one who got approached."

Marcus holds the look.

Marcus: "He came to me."

Darius: "I know. I wanted you to know I know. That wasn't my play — that was somebody under me who I've already handled."

THE SCORE

The Negotiation — Clean Terms and a Disclosure

PROFIT 88 ▲ 8|LOVE 82 ▲ 10|TAX 10 ▼ 6

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + PATH FORWARD — MOVES 02 & 09

Two moves ran at the end of this movement. The Path Forward: the territorial agreement was stated plainly and accepted cleanly — neither party oversold it or added conditions that would make it fragile. Then Darius ran Move 02 — the Honest Strike — by disclosing information he did not have to disclose: that he knew about the approach on Marcus's person, and that it was not his sanctioned play. This disclosure is one of the highest-value moves available in a competitor relationship because it converts potential antagonism into mutual understanding. Darius is telling Marcus: we have the same problem, and I handled mine. The Love score builds because both parties have now extended genuine transparency to the other in a world where transparency is not the default. This competitor relationship has a different character after this conversation than it had before it.

◆

The Family Conversation

The most scored conversation in the street — and the one that almost never goes right

The Family conversation is the hardest conversation in the street because it requires the person who lives in one world to be honest with the person they love about that world, without the protections that the world normally provides. In the street, you control information as a survival skill. In the Family conversation, the person you love is asking for the information you have been most carefully protecting them from.

Jerome's younger brother David has been asking questions. Jerome has been managing the questions for two years. David is nineteen. He has been watching.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE QUESTION THAT CANNOT BE MANAGED
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE QUESTION THAT CANNOT BE MANAGED

David: "I want in."

Jerome was expecting this conversation. He has been managing it with smaller disclosures for two years — giving David enough to feel included, not enough to be implicated. That approach has now ended.

Jerome: "No."

David: "You're going to tell me it's dangerous. I know it's dangerous. I've been watching you do it my whole life. I know what I'm getting into."

Jerome: "You don't."

David: "Then tell me. Stop protecting me from it and tell me."

The ask behind the ask. David is not asking to join the operation. He is asking to be told the truth — to be treated as someone whose understanding matters rather than someone whose ignorance needs to be maintained.

THE SCORE

The Question That Cannot Be Managed — The Real Ask Arrives

PROFIT 54 ▼ 8|LOVE 62 ▲ 4|TAX 44 ▲ 10

MOVE PRESSURE REVEAL — MOVE 06 FROM BELOW

David ran Move 06 from below — he named the real conversation that Jerome had been preventing from happening. "Stop protecting me from it and tell me" is the Pressure Reveal from the less powerful position: naming that the information management has been a protection strategy, and asking for it to end. Jerome's single-word responses — "No." and "You don't." — are not the right moves here. They are the moves of a leader who is still trying to manage the conversation rather than have it. Profit drops because Jerome is not engaging with David's actual request. Love is holding because David's ask is itself an act of Love — he wants to understand his brother's world — but it is under pressure from Jerome's management.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE TRUTH
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE TRUTH

Jerome: "You want the truth?"

David: "Yes."

Jerome: "The truth is I've spent ten years making sure you didn't have to know this. Not because you couldn't handle it. Because the minute you know it — really know it, inside it — you can't unknow it. You can't go back. Your whole life changes what it's allowed to be. I didn't want that for you."

David is quiet.

Jerome: "That's the real answer. It's not about whether you're ready. It's about the fact that I've been trying to give you a life that doesn't have this in it. And if you come in, I lose that. I don't just lose it for you — I lose the reason I've been doing this in the first place."

The most honest thing Jerome has said to his brother. The Love that runs the entire operation — the reason Jerome took the path he took — is now in the room between them, named.

David: "You never told me that."

Jerome: "I know."

THE SCORE

The Truth — The Love Behind the Operation Named

PROFIT 80 ▲ 26|LOVE 96 ▲ 34|TAX 14 ▼ 30

MOVE HONEST STRIKE — MOVE 02

Jerome ran the Honest Strike at the deepest level available to him in this relationship: he named not just the danger of David entering the world, but the specific Love that has been driving Jerome's protection. "I lose the reason I've been doing this in the first place" is the complete disclosure — it tells David that his exclusion from the world was not about David's capacity but about Jerome's motivation. The Love score moves more in this single movement than in any other conversation in this book — 34 points — because both parties are now in the same honest room for the first time in their relationship. The Tax drops 30 points because two years of managed information have been replaced by one complete honest statement. The conversation is not over. But it has arrived at something real.

pages.title: MOVEMENT THREE WHAT COMES NEXT
pages.html:
MOVEMENT THREE WHAT COMES NEXT

David: "I'm not going to stop wanting to understand it."

Jerome: "I know that too."

David: "So what do we do?"

Jerome: "I don't know yet. But I'm not going to manage you anymore. Whatever we decide, we decide it together. That's what I can give you right now."

Not a resolution. A changed position. Jerome has moved from managing David to engaging with David — which is the only move available that has a chance of producing an outcome neither of them will regret.

THE SCORE

What Comes Next — A Changed Position, Not a Resolution

PROFIT 82 ▲ 2|LOVE 92 ▼ 4|TAX 16 ▲ 2

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

The Path Forward in the Family conversation is not a decision — it is a changed relationship to the decision. Jerome's offer — "we decide it together" — is the most Love-consistent move available to him in this moment because it treats David as a person whose agency matters rather than a problem whose exposure needs to be managed. Love drops slightly from its peak because the conversation has not resolved the actual question — David's request is still open. But the account between them has fundamentally changed. Two years of managed information have been replaced, in one conversation, by the commitment to honesty. That is the highest-value exchange available in a Family conversation in the street world. It does not solve the problem. It makes the problem solvable.

◆

The Exit

The most dangerous conversation in the street — and the most necessary one

The exit from the street is the conversation that most people in this world never have correctly — because having it correctly requires disclosing information, naming intentions, and making requests in a context where all three of those things carry risk. The exit that goes wrong is the one that was never had at all.

Marcus has been in it long enough. He has an opportunity — legitimate, real, something he has been building toward for three years. He needs to have the conversation with Dee that ends the relationship with the operation.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE DIRECT ASK
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE DIRECT ASK

Marcus: "I need to talk to you about something. I'm not coming to you with a problem. I'm coming to you with a decision I've already made, and I'm coming to you because you deserve to hear it from me directly."

The framing is precise. Not a negotiation. Not a request for permission. A disclosure of a decision already made, delivered to the person who deserves to receive it first.

Dee: "Talk."

Marcus: "I'm out. I have something I've been building on the side for three years — a legitimate thing, a real business. It's ready. I've been careful and I'm clean and I want to walk away from this while I can do it that way. I'm not running from anything. I'm walking toward something. There's a difference."

Dee is quiet for a long moment.

Dee: "How long have you been building this?"

Marcus: "Three years. The whole time I've been working with you I've been building toward this."

Dee: "You're telling me this now."

Marcus: "I'm telling you now because now is when it's ready. Before now it wasn't real enough to tell."

THE SCORE

The Direct Ask — The Exit Named Correctly

PROFIT 76 ▲ 8|LOVE 74 ▲ 6|TAX 28 ▲ 10

MOVE HONEST STRIKE — MOVE 02

Marcus ran Move 02 at the highest-stakes moment available in the street: the exit conversation. The elements that make this the correct version of the conversation: he named the decision before asking for a response ("a decision I've already made"), he distinguished walking toward something from running from something — which is the distinction that matters most in this world — and he answered the most potentially problematic question ("you're telling me this now") with the honest answer rather than a managed one. Tax builds because the disclosure of three years of parallel work creates an obligation — Dee now knows that Marcus has been operating with a secondary agenda the entire time. But the Tax is lower than it would be if Dee found out any other way. The honest disclosure creates Tax. The discovered deception would have created a crisis.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO DEE'S RESPONSE
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO DEE'S RESPONSE

Dee: "Three years of working for me and building something else. I should be bothered by that."

Marcus: "Are you?"

Dee: "I'm thinking about it."

A long pause. Marcus does not fill it.

Dee: "The way you worked — you were never short, never a problem, never in my business asking for more than what was agreed. What you built on the side — that was yours. I don't have a claim on your outside life."

Marcus: "I ran it that way deliberately. I didn't want there to ever be a reason for you to feel like you were getting less than what we agreed."

Dee: "I know. That's why I'm not bothered."

THE SCORE

Dee's Response — The Exit Accepted

PROFIT 86 ▲ 10|LOVE 82 ▲ 8|TAX 14 ▼ 14

MOVE EVIDENCE MIRROR — MOVE 04

Dee ran Move 04 on himself — he held up the evidence of Marcus's three years and assessed it honestly. "Never short, never a problem, never in my business asking for more than what was agreed" is Dee reviewing the account and finding it clean. The exit is accepted not because Dee is generous but because Marcus structured the three years in a way that produced an account with no outstanding Tax. The way Marcus operated — never short, never a problem — was itself the preparation for the exit conversation. The score at the moment of exit is a direct product of the score at every prior moment. Dee's acceptance is not a gift. It is the return on a three-year investment in a clean account.

pages.title: MOVEMENT THREE THE CLOSE
pages.html:
MOVEMENT THREE THE CLOSE

Dee: "What do you need from me to make the transition clean?"

The most important sentence in the exit conversation. Dee is not asking what he owes Marcus. He is asking what he can do — which is a different position entirely.

Marcus: "Two weeks to close what's open on my end. A conversation with Ray so he knows what's coming and isn't caught off guard. And your word that what I'm doing on the outside doesn't become a problem."

Dee: "Two weeks. I'll talk to Ray myself. And what you're building — that's yours. It has nothing to do with this."

Marcus: "Appreciate it."

Dee: "Build something real."

THE SCORE

The Close — The Exit That Preserves the Account

PROFIT 90 ▲ 4|LOVE 86 ▲ 4|TAX 8 ▼ 6

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

The exit conversation that ends with "build something real" is among the rarest outcomes available in the street — because it requires both parties to have operated well throughout the relationship, and it requires the exit to be disclosed honestly and early enough to be managed rather than discovered. Marcus earned this close in three years of clean work. Dee earned it by being the kind of Connect whose response to a well-executed exit is to facilitate it rather than complicate it. The Path Forward they built together — two weeks, a conversation with Ray, a word on the outside business — is specific enough to be honored and simple enough to execute cleanly. The relationship ends with a higher score than it began with. That is the rarest outcome in this world and the only one worth building toward.

◆

pages.title: PART THREE
pages.html:
PART THREE

The Drills

Score the street line. Every word carries weight.

DRILL 01

"You know how I move."

Score this line delivered by someone establishing their reliability in an early conversation.

ANSWER P +8 · L +10 · T -6

Profit +8, Love +10. This line works because it does not make a claim about reliability — it invites the other party to confirm what they already know. "You know how I move" is the Evidence Mirror run as a statement: I am not telling you who I am, I am reminding you that you have already observed who I am and asking you to apply that knowledge. The line is only as strong as the record it references. If the record is clean, it builds both scores simultaneously. If the record is not clean, the line produces the opposite effect — it draws attention to a gap between the claim and the evidence.

DRILL 02

"I heard what you said. I just need more time."

Score this response from someone who owes and is asking for an extension.

ANSWER P -4 · L -6 · T +14

Tax +14. The problem with this line is its passivity. "I heard what you said" acknowledges without engaging. "I just need more time" asks without specificity. In any scored conversation where obligation is the subject, vagueness is the most expensive move available because it signals that the speaker has not done the work of knowing what they are asking for. Compare to: "I can have half of it Thursday and the rest by the end of the month — I'm not asking you to write it off, just the timing." That version is Move 09 — the Path Forward — run correctly. "I just need more time" is Move 09 attempted and not completed.

DRILL 03

"I'm going to be straight with you."

Score this opener in a high-stakes street conversation.

ANSWER P +4 · L +8 · T -4

Love +8. This opener builds Love because it signals that what follows is intended to be the honest version of the information rather than the managed version. The signal is only valuable if it is kept — if what follows "I'm going to be straight with you" is actually straight. If what follows is managed information that the speaker is presenting as straight, the opener destroys more Love than it built because the gap between the signal and the delivery is legible to any person who is reading the score. Run this opener only when what follows is genuinely straight.

DRILL 04

"That's not on me."

Score this response to a problem that the speaker caused or contributed to.

ANSWER P -10 · L -12 · T +16

Love -12, Tax +16. "That's not on me" is the Ownership Move refused — the moment where accountability was available and was not taken. In the street, where the account between people is tracked with precision, the refusal of accountability for something that is partially or fully yours is one of the highest Tax-producing moves available. It does not just create the Tax of the immediate exchange. It retroactively taxes every prior exchange by introducing the information that this person does not own their part when ownership is costly. The people who were previously in relationship with this person now know something about what those relationships are actually built on.

DRILL 05

"I've been watching you."

Score this line delivered by someone above in the hierarchy to someone below.

ANSWER P +6 · L +12 · T -4

Love +12. This line, from above to below, is one of the highest Love-building moves available in the street because it tells the person below that they have been seen — specifically, by the person whose observation matters most. The street runs on a specific anxiety: the possibility that the work you are doing, the exposure you are taking, the consistency you are maintaining, is invisible to the people who have the power to acknowledge it. "I've been watching you" dissolves that anxiety in three words. It requires no elaboration — the statement itself is complete. The follow-up, if there is one, should be specific. "I've been watching you" followed by a specific observation is Move 04 — Evidence Mirror — at its most complete.

DRILL 06

"Don't put me in the middle of this."

Score this line from a Plug who is being asked to carry a message between two parties in conflict.

ANSWER P +2 · L -8 · T +12

Tax +12. The Plug who refuses to carry becomes a liability in both directions simultaneously. The parties on either side now know that this person's value — which is their willingness to move between positions — has a condition on it. The condition itself is not wrong; there are situations where a Plug is right to decline a carry. The problem is that "don't put me in the middle" as a response to the ask does not explain the condition — it refuses the ask without offering a path. The scored version of this move names the specific reason for the refusal and offers what is available instead: "I can't carry this one — here's who can" or "if you can change this specific element of the ask, I can move it." The refusal without a path creates Tax on both sides of the relationship.

DRILL 07

"My word is good."

Score this line as a closing commitment in a street negotiation.

ANSWER P +4 · L +6 · T -2

Profit +4, Love +6. This line functions as a closing commitment only to the degree that the record behind it supports it. "My word is good" is not a claim about the future — it is a reference to the past, asking the other party to extrapolate from what they have already observed. In the street, the closing commitment that lands is the one that both parties already know is true from experience. The closing commitment from someone whose word has not been established carries zero weight regardless of how it is delivered. Love +6 because the willingness to stake your reputation explicitly on a commitment is itself a Love act — it says: I am putting my name on this and inviting you to hold me to it.

DRILL 08

"I already handled it."

Score this line delivered to someone above who is asking about a problem.

ANSWER P +8 · L +6 · T -8

Profit +8, Tax -8. This is the correct version of the proactive disclosure — compact, decisive, and forward-facing. The person above is asking about a problem. The answer is not an explanation of the problem but a statement that the problem no longer exists. The line works because it respects the above party's time and demonstrates that the speaker did not need direction to resolve the issue — they identified it and addressed it. Compare to: "I wanted to tell you what happened and how I handled it" — same information, three times the words, half the Profit. The street values efficiency in communication because every word is assessed for what it reveals and what it costs.

pages.title: PART FOUR
pages.html:
PART FOUR

The Field Guide

Every street situation. The signal. What it means. Your move.

A NEW PERSON HAS BEEN VOUCHED IN BUT SOMETHING FEELS OFF

WATCH They answer questions before they are fully asked. Their eye contact is calibrated rather than natural. Their story has detail in the wrong places.

MEANS The overcalibrated performance is the signal of someone managing impression rather than being present. Natural confidence in a new environment looks different from performed confidence.

YOUR MOVE Do not confront. Observe. Run Move 08 — the Patience Play. Give them space and watch what they do with it. The person who is performing will fill silence with more performance. The person who is being genuine will let the silence be. The difference becomes clear before the situation becomes consequential.

SOMEONE WHO HAS ALWAYS BEEN SOLID IS SUDDENLY ASKING FOR MORE

WATCH The ask is larger than usual. The reason given is specific but something in the delivery feels managed.

MEANS A person who has been reliable and is now asking for more is usually carrying a Tax account that has reached a level where it is affecting their behavior. The ask is not about the specific thing they are asking for — it is about the underlying condition that produced the ask.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 06 — Pressure Reveal. Not "what do you need the money for" but "what's actually going on with you right now." The answer to the real question changes what your response should be. The person in a temporary situation needs a different response than the person whose fundamental situation has changed.

A CONVERSATION IS MOVING TOO FAST TOWARD COMMITMENT

WATCH The other party is pushing for a decision before you have had time to think. The pressure is not hostile but it is persistent.

MEANS The person who needs an answer before you've had time to form one is managing the quality of your thinking. The urgency itself is information: what are they afraid would happen if you had more time?

YOUR MOVE Run Move 08 — the Patience Play. "Give me a day." The person who cannot give you a day is not giving you a deal — they are giving you a position they need filled before you can evaluate it clearly. The deal that requires your immediate answer is not a deal. It is a managed close.

SOMEONE YOU TRUST TELLS YOU SOMETHING ABOUT A THIRD PERSON THAT CHANGES YOUR READ

WATCH The information is specific and delivered by someone whose intelligence has been reliable. The information, if true, changes what is owed or what is possible.

MEANS Second-hand intelligence in the street is not the same as direct observation. The person delivering the information may have their own interests in how you receive it.

YOUR MOVE Do not act on the information immediately. Run Move 04 — Evidence Mirror — with your own prior observations: does what you are being told match what you have seen? If it matches, the information is probably real. If it conflicts with what you have directly observed, the information may be true in a different context or may be constructed. Verify before you change your position.

THE EXIT IS APPROACHING AND THE CONVERSATIONS ARE GETTING HARDER

WATCH People around you are sensing the change. The small signs of distance — less information shared with you, less investment in your problems — are multiplying.

MEANS The street senses exit before it is announced, and it responds to the sensing by beginning to withdraw what exit would cost it. This is not malicious — it is the natural score movement of relationships that are reading an approaching end.

YOUR MOVE Accelerate the honest conversation. The exit that is sensed but not yet spoken is more expensive than the exit that is named. Move 02 — Honest Strike — with the people who matter: "I need to tell you something. Let me tell you directly." The exit that is handled honestly produces the close that Marcus and Dee achieved. The exit that is sensed and not spoken produces the close that ends worse than it needed to.

In every world, the score is the truth.

The street just doesn't let you pretend otherwise.

The PLT framework applies to every world in this series because the three scores — Profit, Love, Tax — are the actual mechanics of human exchange in every context. What the street reveals is what those mechanics look like when the courtesy layer is removed and the stakes are immediate.

The conversation that is scored correctly in the street produces the same outcomes as the conversation scored correctly in the boardroom, the real estate office, the loan officer's call, the one-on-one. Genuine value exchanged. Genuine regard for the person across from you. Obligations acknowledged and addressed rather than accumulated and detonated. The framework is the same. The cost of getting it wrong is different.

Read the score. In every room. In every world. The score is always running, and the score is always honest, even when the conversation is not.

Profit. Love. Tax.

Every word is a contract.
